episodes.title: What Jensen Huang's Stunning Return Means for the AI Trade
episodes.description: On Monday morning, Nvidia's board stunned the world and announced that it was reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO. Reportedly, President Trump pressed the board to bring back Huang, and his return kicked...
episodes.description_full: On Monday morning, Nvidia's board stunned the world and announced that it was reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO. Reportedly, President Trump pressed the board to bring back Huang, and his return kicked off a historic rally for the chip maker. (Nasdaq 100 futures went up so fast yesterday, they briefly halted trading.) All of this follows a weekend full of doom and gloom; the S&P 500 was entering correction territory last Friday, just days after Anthropic's blockbuster IPO. When we spoke with Alexander 'Alty' Altmann, global head of equities tactical strategies at Barclays, at the end of October, the AI trade was wobbling. Now, a month later, the AI trade seems, at least for now, ascendant, riding an epic rally that few saw coming. Today, we speak with Altmann about how Wall Street is making sense of Jensen's return, why structural issues around AI revenue and financing won't be fixed anytime soon, and if AI is really too big to fail. episodes.description_full:
As the incoming chairman of the Oversight Committee, Representative Robert Garcia will be leading the investigations into the Trump administration’s alleged corruption.

One challenge Democrats like Garcia will face is that there simply is so much to investigate: shady crypto schemes, ballroom donations, lucrative business deals associated with Trump family members, whatever’s been happening in Venezuela. Where do you begin? And how do you deal with an administration you know is going to fight you at every turn?

So I wanted to have Garcia on the show to talk about what — and who — he wants his committee to investigate, and how these investigations fit into the Democrats’ broader strategy as they take back control of Congress.

episodes.title: How Hard Is It to Get Off Antidepressants?
episodes.description: How hard is it to get off antidepressants? Online, patients tell stories of going through hell when they stopped taking antidepressants: dizziness, brain zaps, panic attacks, anxiety and terror. And...
episodes.description_full:
How hard is it to get off antidepressants? Online, patients tell stories of going through hell when they stopped taking antidepressants: dizziness, brain zaps, panic attacks, anxiety and terror. And Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has talked about this, saying members of his family have had a worse time getting off of SSRIs than heroin. But there’s another side to this story: Lots of doctors and psychiatrists say they've been prescribing antidepressants for years and have seen many patients come off the meds with no worries. Plus, they say they have the data on their side. To find out what the science can tell us, we’re joined by Noam Hassenfeld, host of Vox’s Unexplainable, and we hear from psychiatrist Professor Philip Mitchell, Psychopharmacologist Professor David Taylor, training psychiatrist Dr Mark Horowitz, epidemiological psychiatrist Professor Glyn Lewis, and physician Professor Katharine Wallis.

Artificial intelligence has thrown us into a new era of digital...
episodes.description_full:
It's been called a lot of names: “black October,” “bugmageddon,” “the patchpocalypse,” “a new dark age,” “software Beirut.”

Artificial intelligence has thrown us into a new era of digital insecurity, exposing bugs in the foundations of our digital infrastructure, supercharging the capabilities of hackers, and sending companies and governments scrambling in response. The recent outages at the Federal Aviation Administration, Microsoft Outlook, Apple iCloud and Chase bank branches all appear to be part of a frantic effort to upgrade systems in the face of this new reality. The cybersecurity expert Nicole Perlroth says we should expect these kinds of outages to be a “new normal.”

So I wanted to have Perlroth on the show to ask some basic follow-up questions: How long should we expect this “new normal” to last? How much of our digital lives is vulnerable right now? And what should governments, companies and individuals do to protect themselves?

Perlroth was a New York Times cybersecurity reporter for over 10 years. She’s the author of the 2021 book “This Is How They Tell Me the World Ends,” the host of the podcast “To Catch a Thief” and the founder and managing partner of Silver Buckshot Ventures.

episodes.description: Sugar is in everything these days. At least it seems to be. And it’s not just candy - salad dressings, condiments, sandwich bread, even the blandest of cereals have a few grams of sugar. It hasn’t...
episodes.description_full: Sugar is in everything these days. At least it seems to be. And it’s not just candy - salad dressings, condiments, sandwich bread, even the blandest of cereals have a few grams of sugar. It hasn’t always been this way; in fact, our infatuation with sugar is relatively recent in our species’ history. Which raises two questions: 1) how did it get to be this way? and 2) what is this sugar consumption doing to our health? In the first episode of our two-parter on sugar, we’re exploring question #1, tracing the evolution of our relationship with sugar over millennia. We uncover the dark side of our hunger for this sweet substance, which fueled the enslavement of hundreds of thousands of people as countries sought to satisfy their greed. We learn about the changing uses of sugar, from medicine to spice, sculpture to sweetener, and how the utility of sugar changed our consumption, our economy, and our pantry. Through this, we begin to get a sense of the hidden hand sugar has had in shaping our modern world. Journalist Afra Wang has spent a lot of time in mainland China reporting from the country's AI hotbed — in a vibecoding-obsessed town outside of Hangzhou; at the for-profit schools where influencers are teaching everyday people how to use the technology; and the content studios that are pumping out AI microdramas. Despite Nvidia's earnings outlook looking good, and despite the scale of the Anthropic IPO — it's oversubscribed, as you might know — there are so many open questions about the state of the industry right now. Financing the buildout has become increasingly complicated, and the Democrats who won races in the midterms know that data center opposition is a winning issue. Today's episode is a special two-parter that addresses some of these questions. First, we speak with Stanley Lee, the chief product officer at Liquid Compute, and he explains why Wall Street and Silicon Valley seem to be talking past each other, and what fragilities are emerging in the credit market for GPUs. All those charts that show rising GPU rental rates, Lee tells us, might not be as industry-bullish as they first appear. Then, we turn to Paul Kedrosky, a managing partner at SK Ventures, to discuss why “number goes up and to the right” does not necessarily prove the viability of the capex involved in the AI buildout, and also if Nvidia will remain the central bank for AI. episodes.description_full: In AI’s developmental years, its network architecture created a bottleneck that limited its capabilities. Then researchers tried a mathematical operation referred to as “attention” that allowed AIs to link words and build context. It turbocharged large language models and changed the landscape forever.On this episode of The Quanta Podcast, host Hannah Waters speaks with writer Natalie Wolchover about “attention” — what this attention mechanism is exactly, why machine translation was the task that unlocked it all, and what it can tell us about human intelligence.This topic was covered in a recent story for Quanta Magazine.  Each week on The Quanta Podcast, Quanta Magazine editor-in-chief Samir Patel and Senior Editor Hannah Waters speak with the people behind the award-winning publication to navigate through some of the most important and mind-expanding questions in science and math.

episodes.description_full: This week, we got news that the Trump administration is reportedly considering a requirement for US companies to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models. Any effort to discourage US businesses from using Chinese open-source could be a big deal for both the AI industry and the market, where investors are still debating whether customers will ultimately be willing to pay for pricier homegrown frontier models versus cheaper alternatives. Everyone remembers last year's 'DeepSeek moment' for AI, when a Chinese company released a cheaper model that seemed nearly as good as cutting-edge US ones. So why do businesses actually use open-source? And what are the considerations that take into account in doing so? In this episode, we talk to Daniel Saedi, co-founder of Minerva, to better understand how an AI native company chooses its models. He breaks down how exactly his company mixes and matches models for specific use cases, the risk of abliterated models, and the issue of data sovereignty. episodes.description_full: Edward Said brought the question of Palestine into the American mainstream decades ago. He taught at Columbia University for nearly 40 years, and today, more than two decades after his death, the campus is still reeling from that massive pro-Palestine student protest movement that invoked his name in 2024-2025. The question of Palestine figured heavily into this year’s U.S midterm elections, as growing scrutiny of the U.S.–Israel relationship reached a fever pitch. On this episode we explore the life of Edward Said: the man who pushed for recognition of the Palestinian perspective, the pushback he got, and the dangerous dynamics he foresaw that pave the path to today. episodes.description_full: It took over a decade to make Grand Theft Auto VI. And when it's released on November 19, it will have likely already set at least one record: the most expensive video game ever made. In the years since the last GTA release, the video game industry has changed massively. Investors, once excited by the prospect of blockbuster video games, have pulled back, sales have stagnated, and the industry as a whole seems more precarious. Bloomberg News video game reporter Jason Schreier has been following Rockstar Games and its quest to release GTA VI for a long time.
